Third, the benefits are conditional on regional roles and institutions: exporting regions respond mainly through green technology upgrading, importing regions through clean-electricity availability, and stronger environmental regulation amplifies the transition-promoting association. Grid expansion alone is therefore not sufficient for decarbonization. Transmission investment should be coordinated with storage deployment, regionally differentiated industrial policy, and environmental governance.

title: Assessing consumer choice projections in energy system models: A heat pump case study
abstract: Consumer adoption of heat pumps is a critical component of uncertainty in load growth forecasts, yet projections of heat pump adoption are rarely a focus of deeper investigation. This paper conducts a case study assessment of the structure, outputs, and performance of a model of U.S. residential heat pump adoption that has been used in multiple buildings sector potential studies and cross-sectoral energy system modeling exercises. The assessment includes model sensitivity testing based on a review of key factors in the heat pump adoption literature. Model projections across a range of scenarios show substantial regional variation in projected heat pump sales shares and sensitivity to input adjustments, with sales shares generally higher and less sensitive to input changes in warmer regions with high existing heat pump penetration, and generally lower and more sensitive in colder regions with a large installed base of fossil- and/or resistance-based heating equipment. Model benchmarking shows good agreement between estimated vs. reported heat pump sales and fuel switching shares in 2020 at the national level, but a tendency to underestimate heat pump sales shares vs. historical benchmarks at the state and regional levels. Key limitations are noted in the coverage and depth of existing historical equipment sales datasets, particularly at the state level. The analysis illustrates the current state of the art in projecting U.S. heat pump adoption and highlights key opportunities for improving confidence in heat pump projections within larger load growth forecasts and energy system modeling efforts.

title: A multi-dimensional framework for modeling energy system transition resilience
abstract: Energy system transitions are multi-dimensional processes and are subject to deep uncertainties and vulnerable to shocks. Energy system models have been used to evaluate system resilience to disruptions, mainly from technical and economic perspectives. In this study, we develop a multi-dimensional framework for modeling energy system transition resilience that aligns cross-disciplinary resilience concepts with what energy system models can credibly quantify over long time horizons. Building on existing frameworks and the body of literature, we assemble a coherent set of system performance measures and resilience indicators that track how outcomes evolve under shock. For the proof of concept, we demonstrate the framework with FINTIMES, a bottom-up cost optimization model for Finland, by stress-testing the system with alternative strategies under hypothetical shocks. The stylized analysis shows that resilience is inherently multi-dimensional: gains in affordability or price stability may coincide with weaker social and ecological performances. The results suggest that single-dimensional, single-metric evaluations of resilience are increasingly obsolete in complex, long-term energy system settings because they ignore critical trade-offs. Indicators designed to capture the same aspect of resilience may also yield conflicting signals, underscoring the need to report a comprehensive set of indicators and interpret them jointly. In addition, resilience conclusions depend on shock characteristics (e.g., intensity and duration) and on strategic choices; a strategy that strengthens technical and some economic measures can simultaneously deteriorate social, ecological, and other economic outcomes. Finally, the framework structure is applicable for comparable contexts, supporting policy design by surfacing the trade-offs involved.

title: Optimizing off-grid residential hybrid systems with and without energy storage: A constriction-coefficient PSO approach to cost, reliability, and emissions trade-offs
abstract: In response to the growing demand for sustainable and cost-effective energy solutions, hybrid energy systems that integrate solar, wind, and diesel generators provide an alternative to diesel-only supply for residential buildings, particularly in remote areas. This study examines the optimal design and performance of five stand-alone hybrid systems, with and without battery energy storage (BES), with emphasis on reliability, cost, and environmental impact. An improved constriction-coefficient Particle Swarm Optimization (ICC-PSO) method is proposed for system optimization, and its performance is compared with Harmony Search, Simulated Annealing, standard PSO, and five PSO variants. The effects of reliability limits, fuel price, photovoltaic cost, and CO 2 emission penalties are also examined. The results show that the solar/BES/diesel configuration reduces total net annual cost (TNAC) by up to 36.6% and CO 2 emissions by 61.7% relative to diesel-only, while maintaining high reliability. Across the tested cases, ICC-PSO yields lower TNAC and faster convergence than the benchmarked algorithms. These findings indicate that battery-integrated hybrid systems can support off-grid residential energy planning under varying economic, policy, and reliability conditions.

title: Materials in energy system modelling: A review and integrated energy–material framework for circular economy and decarbonisation pathways
abstract: Achieving climate neutrality requires transforming both energy and material systems. Energy system models (ESMs) are central to assessing decarbonisation pathways, yet they lack a consistent representation of material dynamics, limiting their ability to capture material-related energy demand and the role of circular economy (CE) strategies in reducing it. Material flow analysis (MFA), on the other hand, provides a detailed representation of material stocks, flows, and circularity, enabling the assessment of material system evolution, but does not explicitly capture the associated energy demand, emissions, and broader energy system implications. This study presents a review of how industrial sectors, material flows, supply chains, and CE strategies are represented in ESMs. Based on this assessment, three state-of-the-art models, FORECAST, IESA-Opt, and IMAGE-TIMER, are reviewed in greater detail. The review reveals that, despite recent improvements in industrial representation and the inclusion of CE strategies, inter-sector material supply chains are rarely modelled, leading to inconsistencies in associated energy demand representation, while CE elements remain largely fragmented and exogenous. Building on these findings, we introduce dynamic MFA (dMFA) as a complementary approach for representing materials and develop a conceptual integrated ESM-MFA framework. The framework identifies explicit interlinkage points, clarifies their functional roles, and maps CE strategies to appropriate modelling components. It aligns material demand with production and enables a consistent estimation of material-related energy use and emissions within energy system modelling, while also highlighting key methodological challenges associated with integration. Overall, the framework strengthens the assessment of the energy transition and supports integrated energy-material scenario development, enabling circularity-informed decarbonisation pathways.

title: Modeling the potential impact of storage on the US power sector in a multisector dynamic context
abstract: The electric power sector is expected to grow in size, importance, and complexity around the world as economies expand and electric supply technologies and demand patterns evolve in significant ways. Newer, rapidly growing sectors could alter the temporal profile of electricity demand from historical patterns. In addition, substantial increases in variable renewable energy technologies could occur, adding variability and uncertainty to the diurnal and seasonal profile of electric supply. In this context, the emergence of modular, flexible electricity storage technologies may have profound impacts on the structure and operation of electric power systems. Here we address a gap in multi-sector dynamics models by incorporating grid-based electricity storage investment and operation into the electric sector dynamics of the Global Change Analysis Model-USA (GCAM-USA). We find a potentially significant role for storage technologies in the future of the U.S. power system, with storage capacity ranging from 196.1 to 372.4 GW (5.0 to 10.6%) of capacity in 2050 and 352.1 to 802.6 GW (6.0 to 9.0%) in 2100 across several techno-economic scenarios. We also find that storage can help to smooth variability in residual load arising from evolving electricity demands and the introduction of high shares of variable renewable energy to the electric grid. This reduces reliance on high-cost peaking generators, improves utilization of base-load technologies, increases system-wide capacity factors, and limits curtailment of renewable generation.

title: Underground hydrogen storage site suitability from the views of efficiency, cost, and risk — A site selection framework for decision-makers
abstract: Underground Hydrogen Storage (UHS) in porous media is emerging as a key enabler of large-scale, long-duration energy storage to support net-zero energy systems. However, determining suitable storage sites remains a complex, multidisciplinary challenge based on the integration of technical, economic, and risk-related considerations, often leaving an abstract “black-box” impression to non-specialists such as policy stakeholders and the public. This study presents a transparent and easy-to-grasp conceptual framework for UHS site suitability assessment, built around three interdependent pillars: efficiency, cost, and risk. Each is assessed using proxy parameters—such as permeability, depth, and well density—and combined into a unified visual model that defines a “suitability zone” representing the unified conditions under which all three aspects meet project requirements. The applicability of the framework is demonstrated by assessing a set of oil and gas fields in the Irish Sea Basin, resulting in the identification of ‘suitable sites’ for UHS that satisfy minimum thresholds across all criteria representing the three aspects. The conceptual framework supports transparent and structured decision-making by making explicit how geological, operational, and contextual factors interact to determine site suitability. The proposed approach offers a flexible and transferable decision-support tool for early-stage UHS project screening, ranking, and investment prioritisation. It is also adaptable to other subsurface technologies such as the storage of carbon dioxide and natural gas, and geothermal energy storage.

title: The role of controllable household appliances for effective uptake of digital services by consumers and communities in the energy transition
abstract: Digitalisation is transforming modern energy systems into complex socio-technical ecosystems where interconnected devices, user practices and governance structures must be considered together. To analyse this landscape and address relevant research questions concerning controllable household appliances, a multilevel conceptual framework has been developed by organising the investigation into five interconnected thematic domains: digital control of the appliances, flexibility analysis, user engagement, management by aggregators, and relations with energy communities. Through discussions of selected scientific articles and real-world projects, this article reviews the categorisation of household appliances, methods for controlling them, and indicators to assess load-shifting capabilities and flexibility. It then addresses user engagement based on users’ behaviour, active role, and comfort. Operational strategies for aggregators are identified to manage controllable appliances, develop suitable business models, and participate in flexibility markets. Finally, the deployment of smart household appliances within energy communities is discussed as a further opportunity to involve more users and share their available resources. The synthesis distinguishes comparatively established approaches from promising but still weakly validated combinations of appliance types, control strategies, engagement mechanisms, and aggregator models.

title: Corrigendum to “Vehicle-to-grid energy technologies: A patent landscape analysis and technology updates” [Energy Strategy Rev. 66 (2026) 102316, pp.1-21]
Can the new energy demonstration city pilot boost energy justice? A spatial difference-in-differences analysis
abstract: Energy justice is central to achieving a fair and inclusive energy transition. Using balanced panel data for 282 prefecture-level cities in China from 2010 to 2022, this study employs a spatial difference-in-differences approach to examine the relationship between New Energy Demonstration City pilot designation and urban energy justice while accounting for inter-city spatial spillovers. The analysis yields three main findings. First, the SDID estimates suggest that NEDC pilot designation is associated with higher local energy justice, while the spatial estimates indicate positive cumulative spillovers across spatially connected cities. Second, industrial structure upgrading and regional development inequality moderate the estimated policy relationships in different ways, with industrial structure upgrading strengthening both the local relationship and spatial spillovers, whereas regional development inequality weakens the local relationship but has no significant moderating effect on spatial spillovers. Third, the local estimates are relatively larger in eastern and central regions and in large cities, while the estimated spatial spillovers are stronger in resource-based cities and cities with higher renewable energy endowments. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating spatial linkages and local development conditions into the design and evaluation of new energy policies aimed at advancing energy justice.

title: Retraction notice to “Energy consumption prediction for households in a society with an ageing population” [Energy Strategy Rev. 57 (2025) 101622]
Retraction notice to “Diversification of structural and crisis risks in the energy sector of the ASEAN member countries” [Energy Strategy Rev. 35 (2021) 100655]
The burden of the “Silver Wave”: How the hukou system moderates the impact of aging on household energy consumption
abstract: Population ageing is increasingly reshaping the consumption structure of urban energy technologies, yet its household-level implications remain poorly understood. Using micro-level survey and interview data from 2050 households in Beijing, this study examines how the age of the household head shapes per capita household energy consumption, and how these effects are conditioned by intra-urban spatial structure and China's hukou system. We find pronounced intergenerational differences in household energy consumption and associated socio-technical impact outcomes. Electricity and natural gas dominate the energy mix, with electricity consumption rising systematically with age, reflecting more home-centred daily routines, longer television-viewing time, and differences in appliance conditions. Older household heads are also more likely to be retired or not working, to occupy larger floor area on a per capita basis, and to live in dwellings with weaker thermal conditions. Age-related effects are most pronounced in the core area, where older residents are more concentrated and older housing stock with weaker dwelling conditions is more prevalent. Institutional status further amplifies these patterns: local hukou significantly strengthens the association between age and household energy consumption. Together, the findings show that the energy implications of population ageing emerge from the interaction of demographic change, spatial context and institutional stratification, underscoring the need for differentiated urban energy strategies that support affordable and clean energy consumption in ageing cities.

title: Statistical validation of geothermal development stages: A strategic benchmarking framework for energy policy and market maturity
abstract: Limiting energy-system emissions increases the strategic value of reliable renewable sources. Geothermal energy stands out for its high capacity factor and low emissions, yet its historical deployment is often described through visually defined periods rather than statistically dated regimes. This study develops a data-driven framework to statistically validate geothermal development stages and benchmark major markets against a reference pathway. Using annual cumulative installed capacity for leading countries (1945–2024), we estimate endogenous break dates with the Bai–Perron multiple structural change methodology and summarize global diffusion via a sample-aggregate series. An ACC–ACA visualization highlights long-run growth and volatility. Country trajectories are benchmarked to the U.S. reference market through correlation-based time-shift alignment and stage-by-stage similarity scores; Dynamic Time Warping distances serve as a robustness diagnostic. The U.S. series shows five statistically identified breaks over 1960–2024, including a post-2015 regime of moderated growth. The sample-aggregate series displays three breaks (1977, 1989, 2012) with accelerated expansion after 2012. Benchmarking reveals heterogeneous pathways, ranging from strong multi-stage similarity (Italy, Japan) through partial alignment with weaker late-stage recovery (Mexico, Philippines) to limited stage completion (Iceland, Türkiye). The statistically dated staging and alignment framework provides a replicable basis for interpreting geothermal deployment pathways, informing national energy strategies, and supporting policy design for accelerated clean-energy transitions under SDG 7.

title: Strategic pathways for scaling virtual power plants: A global comparative review and the VPP institutional transition framework (VITF)
abstract: Virtual power plants (VPPs) aggregate distributed energy resources into system-facing flexibility portfolios, yet deployment remains uneven across jurisdictions. This study examines institutional conditions associated with durable VPP deployment through an exploratory comparative review of 26 cases across six continents. The VPP Institutional Transition Framework (VITF) evaluates five dimensions—aggregator recognition, market or procurement access, remuneration design, governance coherence, and pilot-to-durable transition design—and separates four institutional stages from three strategic pathways: Project/Sandbox-to-Market, Programmatic-to-Market, and Durable Procurement or Administrative Embedding. We assessed cases through standardized evidence extraction, independent LLM-assisted preliminary coding, author adjudication, and sensitivity analysis. Twelve cases are Stage 1, ten Stage 2, and four Stage 3; none meet the Stage 0 definition. Two high-scoring cases remain Stage 2 because Stage 3 requires formal recognition and repeatable access. Five cases follow Pathway A, three Pathway B, and four Pathway C, while 14 remain pathway indeterminate; four of five Pathway A routes are retrospective. Remuneration design has the lowest mean (1.27), reflecting the absence of service-linked payment in most Stage 1 cases. Comparable PV–battery configurations occur across all occupied stages, while more durable cases are characterized by recognized authority, recurring access, service-linked remuneration, coherent governance, and either a documented transition mechanism or durable endpoint. Durable institutionalization can therefore occur without open-market integration. The VITF provides a reproducible institutional diagnostic and transition framework for identifying first-order weaknesses, distinguishing current institutional position from routes to durable endpoints, and assessing the institutional basis for VPP contributions to flexibility, resilience, and energy security.

title: Virtual Power Plants for DER integration: A comprehensive review of aggregation, control, market participation and revenue allocation
abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) poses significant challenges to power systems due to their intermittent, fluctuating, and stochastic characteristics. Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) have emerged as a promising solution by enabling the aggregation and management of DERs to provide reliable and flexible energy services. This review presents a systematic analysis of VPPs, covering DER aggregation, coordinated control, market participation, and revenue allocation. First, DERs are classified and their modeling approaches are examined, highlighting the difficulties in accurately representing operational characteristics and inherent uncertainties. Various aggregation methods are comparatively analyzed to evaluate their contributions to scalability, flexibility, and operational efficiency. Subsequently, centralized, distributed, and hybrid coordinated control structures are reviewed, together with multi-time-scale optimization strategies integrating day-ahead scheduling, intra-day adjustment, and real-time operation. The review further investigates VPP participation in energy, ancillary service, and local flexibility markets through price- and quantity-based bidding mechanisms, as well as emerging business models for monetizing aggregated DERs. In addition, representative revenue allocation methods are reviewed and compared, emphasizing that balancing fairness, incentive compatibility, and computational efficiency remains a major challenge for sustainable VPP commercialization. Compared with existing reviews, this paper develops an integrated analytical framework linking technical coordination and market interaction in VPPs, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the progression from resource aggregation to market-oriented operation. Finally, key challenges and future research directions are identified to support the reliable and economically viable development of VPPs in low-carbon energy systems.

title: Strategic appraisal of energy storage for renewable integration: KPI-MCDM/A evidence mapping, a feasibility-first workflow, and minimum reporting standards
abstract: Energy storage is central to renewable-energy integration and to strategic planning for low-carbon energy systems with high shares of variable renewables. Yet decision-oriented evidence remains fragmented across technology domains and metric systems, and links between storage technologies, KPI emphases, and MCDM/A method choices are rarely synthesized within a unified and reproducible framework. To address this gap, this study combines bibliometric evidence mapping with a standardized coding workflow that consolidates indicators into five KPI dimensions and major MCDM/A method families. Document-level co-occurrence analysis of titles, abstracts, and author keywords is applied to a curated dataset of 301 publications (2000-2025) spanning electrochemical and battery, mechanical, thermal, and hydrogen/chemical storage. The results show accelerated growth of assessment research and a clear shift toward strategic decision and planning framings in which selection, optimization, and multi-criteria evaluation are increasingly central. Coupling patterns reveal dominant emphases on techno-economic feasibility and system integration, whereas social-safety criteria remain unevenly operationalized, particularly for mechanical and thermal storage. Method use is highly concentrated, with fuzzy approaches, AHP, and TOPSIS forming a prevailing core toolbox, while structure-aware approaches capable of representing inter-criteria dependence and non-compensatory feasibility bottlenecks remain sparsely adopted. Beyond mapping, the study delivers deployment-relevant guidance through a feasibility-first decision workflow and minimum reporting standards designed to improve auditability, cross-study comparability, and strategic relevance in energy-storage appraisal.

title: An integrated techno-economic and leakage-sensitive environmental framework for crop-residue biogas systems: Application to Cameroon
abstract: Crop-residue anaerobic digestion offers a scalable pathway to simultaneously address agricultural waste mismanagement and clean cooking deficits across sub-Saharan Africa, yet credible regional assessments that combine auditable capital-cost modelling with leakage-sensitive environmental accounting are absent from the literature. This study develops a regionally resolved techno-economic and environmental framework for crop-residue valorization via anaerobic digestion, applied in Cameroon as a proof of concept for residue-rich economies. An empirically calibrated, cross-validated CAPEX scaling model (105–43,835 m 3 ), explicit logistics scenarios, and leakage-conditional environmental accounting are integrated across ten regions (2016–2020). Recoverable residues averaged 2.11 Mt yr −1 , yielding ∼0.605 billion m 3 yr −1 biogas. Plant-gate levelized cost ranged from 0.034 to 0.049 USD m −3 , with approximately 78% of national biogas potential below 0.045 USD m −3 . Net climate benefit reached +503 ktCO 2 e yr −1 under LPG displacement; the break-even methane leakage threshold falls to ∼4.5% under the observed cooking-fuel mix. Substantial air-quality co-benefits persist across the methane-leakage scenarios evaluated, conditional on displacement of polluting cooking fuels. The framework provides a replicable circular economy planning tool connecting agricultural waste valorization, clean energy access, climate performance, and nutrient recycling for data-constrained developing economies.

title: Green bonds and renewable energy investment in China: Implications for sustainable development
abstract: China has emerged as the world's largest issuer of green bonds, raising critical questions about the extent to which this financial instrument catalyzes real renewable energy investment and advances sustainable development goals. This study examines the dynamic relationship between green bond issuance and renewable energy investment across China's provincial panel over the period 2016 to 2023. Using a two-way fixed-effects panel regression augmented by the Driscoll-Kraay estimator for cross-sectional dependence, and a Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel causality test, this paper provides robust empirical evidence that green bond issuance exerts a statistically significant and economically meaningful positive effect on renewable energy capital formation. A one-standard-deviation increase in provincial green bond issuance is associated with a 31.2 percent rise in renewable energy investment after controlling for GDP per capita, trade openness, foreign direct investment, energy prices, and policy uncertainty. The greenium, defined as the yield differential between green and conventional bonds of equivalent maturity, averages 18 to 22 basis points, confirming investor demand for sustainable assets. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that eastern coastal provinces benefit disproportionately, while central and western regions exhibit weaker transmission owing to institutional deficiencies and underdeveloped capital markets. The findings carry direct policy relevance for China's dual carbon targets and for emerging market economies seeking to replicate the Chinese green finance model. Recommendations encompass unified certification standards, regional green finance development zones, and mandatory green use-of-proceeds disclosure.

title: Technologies and approaches for grid integration of distributed and decentralized energy resources
abstract: There is a need for advanced design and operational strategies as well as technologies to optimize integration of Distributed Energy Resources (DERs) to the power systems for maximum profits and reduce emissions. Renewable energy sources which dominate the decentralized and distributed energy resources are generally associated with intermittence and are stochastic in nature, hence they need for optimal energy management strategies for system reliability and operational efficiency. The integration of DERs is associated with multiple technical challenges in terms of grid stability, quality of power, and the need for robust control and communication systems. This study examines and synthesizes the various energy resources, conversion technologies, integration techniques, and scalability factors associated DER integration in smart grid and micro-grids as well as the traditional grid and presents different technologies and measures for enhanced grid integration of decentralized and distributed energy sources in grids and micro grids. The study showed that maximum grid integration of DERs provides several benefits, like enhanced reliability better power quality, higher efficiency and enhanced energy independence. The various integration methods include grid scale storage, integration of the cellular approach in the energy system planning and operation, use of virtual power plant concepts, use of V2G technologies and electrification of transport, application of demand side measures and demand response, use of both on grid and off grid/islanded microgrids, use of smart grid features and infrastructure for both main grids and micro grids by upgrading the traditional grids and micro grids, and application energy management and optimization tools and techniques. Integration measures include voltage regulation at substation level, backup generators at distribution networks, creation of express feeders, use of supervisory control systems, grid scale storage on distribution networks, use of advanced planning and management tool and modernization of the grid with smart features in the long-term. The study recommends among others future studies in evolving smart grid integration technologies and capabilities and development of policy measures to transform the traditional grid to a smart grid with two-way flow of communication and power.

title: Economic-financial and technical challenges in the operation of power systems with the integration of variable renewable energy: A systematic literature review
abstract: In this study, we investigate the principal economic, financial, and technical challenges in the operation of electricity markets arising from the integration of variable renewable energy (VRE), specifically solar photovoltaic and wind power, and evaluate the role of regulation in addressing these challenges. VRE affects both short-term power system operation and long-term investment conditions. The main contribution of this work is to reduce the prevailing fragmentation in the literature by systematically linking technical constraints with economic and financial requirements. To this end, we propose a challenge–service–instrument framework designed to support context-specific energy strategies and regulatory design. Methodologically, we implement a qualitative and quantitative keyword co-occurrence protocol applied to a corpus of 91 articles, systematically selected from scientific databases and published between 2016 and 2027. The results reveal a methodological disconnect in existing literature and show that VRE intermittency is rarely analyzed jointly with other relevant factors. Consequently, this study advances an integrative perspective that traces how technical constraints (e.g., inertia and system stability) translate into economic and financial requirements for firmness, thereby necessitating specific regulatory instruments (e.g., capacity mechanisms) to safeguard the viability of the energy transition.

title: Resilience in energy systems – A systematic review of definitions, characteristics and metrics as a system-specific framework for different assessment approaches and resilience functions
abstract: Resilience in energy systems has become a highly discussed topic recently. However, there is a lack of common understanding concerning its definition and quantification. While prior works state these shortcomings, there is in addition a relevant effect on long-term planning which needs to take into consideration resilience approaches to account not only for both power and energy balance. However, at the first instance there is the requirement to define how the different aspects and dimensions of resilience as well as existing metrics for energy systems are derived. Furthermore, assessment approaches are sensitive to system boundaries, system-specific characteristics and resilience functions (i.e. the desired system objectives) that need to be accounted for, as it is a main reason for differing metrics. Therefore, this review paper draws attention to definitions, characteristics and quantification approaches for different system-specific settings and functions to fill the gaps of previous publications. The approach pursued to define resilience assessments first determines various dimensions of resilience functions based on the classic target triangle of the energy economics at the highest level of aggregation (security of supply, cost efficiency and environmental protection). The comprehensive literature review shows that different issues have been examined in varying degrees of depth. Derived from this, a theoretical concept is defined and existing metrics to quantify resilience are categorized. It intends to evaluate existing appropriate methodologies for the individual use case, to serve as a tool to identify system-characteristics based assessments and to motivate methodologies for system types currently missing in assessment approaches.

title: Harnessing Nepal's surplus hydropower: Comparative economics of green hydrogen and other energy storage options
IoT-enabled microgrids for energy management and demand response: A review and future trends
abstract: The rapid advancement of digital energy infrastructures has accelerated the transition toward internet of things (IoT)-enabled microgrids capable of autonomous monitoring, coordination, and optimization of distributed resources. By integrating sensing, communication, and intelligent control, microgrids can enhance local energy management, support demand-side flexibility, and interact effectively with higher-level grid operations. This paper presents a comprehensive review of recent developments in IoT-assisted energy management strategies within microgrids, with particular emphasis on demand response (DR) mechanisms and price-aware operational scheduling. The text looks at various applications within residential sectors, such as the coordination of smart appliances, distributed energy generation, and the integration of electric vehicles (EVs). It emphasizes the role that bidirectional charging technologies, including vehicle-to-grid (V2G) and grid-to-vehicle (G2V), play in promoting cost-effective and reliable operations. Existing studies have extensively investigated IoT-integrated DR through real-time load monitoring, automated appliance scheduling, dynamic pricing, EV coordination, and optimization-based energy management. However, the practical deployment of these approaches remains constrained by heterogeneous communication protocols and devices, the secure collection and processing of large volumes of real-time data, and the computational and operational complexity associated with coordinating multiple distributed resources. The review assesses communication architectures, optimization methods, and control platforms that support scalable and interoperable microgrid operations. It discusses key challenges related to interoperability, data management, and system complexity. Additionally, it explores emerging trends such as AI-driven decision-making, decentralized control paradigms, and adaptive IoT frameworks, which are promising directions for future research and implementation.

title: Attention-based deep learning framework for battery charge, health, and lifetime estimation in lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles
abstract: The need to ensure Li-ion batteries are long-lasting, reliable, secure, and efficient is growing as the use of Electric Vehicles (EVs) rises. Despite advantages like higher energy density, faster charging, and environmental benefits such as reduced carbon emissions, lower air pollution, and less noise pollution, their major challenges, like performance degradation, safety concerns, and life span prediction, pose a need for a robust Battery Management System (BMS) together with methodologies for the prediction of their state parameters. A hybrid simulation and data-driven approach for the unified prediction of Li-ion batteries' State of Charge (SOC), State of Health (SOH), and Remaining Useful Life (RUL) is presented in this research. A Panasonic NCR18650BD Li-ion battery has been tested, using electrical and thermal elements to provide an extensive dataset of charge/discharge and degradation characteristics. After processing the simulated data in Python, an LSTM Attention-Augmented network approach has been proposed to capture the short- and long-term temporal dependencies of battery dynamics. For SOC, SOH, and RUL estimation, the superior estimation performance of the recommended model results in Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) values of 0.0091, 0.00127, and 0.00123, respectively, which correspond to coefficients of determination (R 2 ) of 0.9976, 0.9998, and 0.9989. Validation using the NASA battery aging dataset shows the applicability of the proposed framework to experimentally measured battery data and provides supporting evidence of its potential generalization capability under real-world operating scenarios. It can be observed that the proposed attention-based LSTM network efficiently integrates simulation and data-driven learning for reliable multi-state estimation, offering a scalable solution for advanced predictive BMS applications.

title: Renewable energy clusters and local economic development in China: Innovation and employment effects
abstract: This paper examines whether renewable energy clusters generate measurable innovation spillovers and employment gains across Chinese prefectural-level cities. China has emerged as the world's largest producer and installer of renewable energy capacity, yet evidence on the local economic consequences of geographic clustering in this sector remains thin. Using a panel of 284 Chinese prefecture-level cities observed annually from 2005 to 2022, we combine a spatial Durbin model with a two-way fixed effects estimator to identify within-city and cross-city effects. We instrument cluster formation using provincial feed-in-tariff policy adoption to address reverse causality between local economic conditions and cluster emergence. Results show that a one-standard-deviation increase in cluster intensity raises local patent filings by 8.3 percent and renewable-sector employment by 6.1 percent. Positive spillovers extend to neighboring cities within 300 km, confirming knowledge diffusion beyond cluster boundaries. Heterogeneity analysis reveals that effects are stronger in cities with higher human capital stocks and better transport infrastructure. The findings carry direct implications for China's dual-carbon target and for industrial policy design in middle-income economies undertaking green transitions.

title: Is energy security compatible with sustainability? A structural system analysis
abstract: This study examines whether energy security is structurally compatible with environmental sustainability under contemporary energy transition pathways. Using an unbalanced panel of 112 countries over 2000–2023, we estimate a three-stage least-squares system linking energy security, greenhouse gas emissions, and sustainability performance. Compatibility is defined as a positive and statistically distinguishable total effect of energy security on sustainability operating through emissions, conditional on the renewable energy share. In the full sample, stronger energy security is associated with higher emissions, while emissions reduce sustainability performance, resulting in a negative total effect at the mean renewable share. The relationship nevertheless differs across country groups. Among OECD countries, renewable penetration attenuates the emissions response to improved energy security, and the resulting total effect is smaller and only marginally distinguishable from zero, indicating movement toward, but not the achievement of, compatibility. In the EU-28, renewable penetration is directly associated with stronger energy security and lower emissions, although it does not significantly moderate the security–emissions relationship. By contrast, renewable penetration strengthens rather than weakens the emissions response in the full and non-OECD samples. These findings show that renewable deployment can facilitate the alignment of energy security and environmental objectives through different channels, but a higher renewable share alone is insufficient to secure compatibility. Its contribution depends on the composition of renewable deployment and its integration into the wider energy system.

title: How to promote new energy power generation: Research on the operation strategy of virtual power plant with the participation of computing power enterprises
abstract: In the context of power market development, the power demand of computing power enterprises is on the rise. As an important link, the operation mode of virtual power plants (VPP) affects the power market and the growth of new energy power generation, and is restricted by many factors, such as thermal power costs. From the perspective of the power supply chain, this paper establishes a model that includes energy producers, VPP (Power Type, Load Type, and Energy Type) and computing power enterprises, introduces the differential game strategy, and studies the impact of different factors on new energy power generation. The study found that the increase in new energy subsidies had a significant impact on the proportion of new energy power generation in the power mix, and the subsidy policy was an important means to promote new energy power generation, but excessive dependence on it should be avoided. The change in thermal power costs affects the generation decisions of green power enterprises and the operation strategies of VPP, and market regulation needs to be comprehensively considered. Different types of VPP have different sensitivities to operation and maintenance costs as well as penalty and loss costs. Power Type, Load Type, and Energy Type VPP each have their own applicable scenarios and advantages.

title: Designed for a secure transition – a systematic review of supply security in energy system models
abstract: While renewable electricity has gained traction, the transition to a low-carbon energy system is still subject to large uncertainties about future energy use and supply portfolios. In the light of recent disruptive events such as geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions, it is evident that energy transition strategies should consider unforeseen disturbances. In this paper, we conduct a systematic review of 179 energy system modelling studies from Scopus and Web of Science based on the PRISMA guidelines. We include articles considering various aspects of energy security, focusing on large-scale system models with a long-term techno-economic design perspective. Our analysis reveals significant variation among studies in three key areas: the security aspects evaluated, the types of disruptions considered, and the methodological approaches employed. While weather variability is commonly examined, other security threats such as climate change or geopolitical disruptions receive less attention.

title: Electrification pathways for passenger cars: A comparative analysis of China and Europe
abstract: China and Europe have made significant progress in the electrification of mobility, but they differ substantially in their policy approaches and institutional frameworks. This paper presents a comparative analysis of their electrification pathways, focusing on the motivations, policy strategies, and challenges associated with scaling up electric-vehicle adoption. The study aims to: (i) examine the policy measures implemented in each region; (ii) assess outcomes in terms of market growth, infrastructure development, and industrial competitiveness; and (iii) identify key similarities and differences while deriving lessons to support transport-sector decarbonization. The comparison of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and comparable diesel vehicles shows substantial regional differences in economic competitiveness. Based on Total Cost of Ownership analysis, BEVs are approximately 17% cheaper than diesel vehicles in China, while diesel vehicles remain about 25% cheaper than BEVs in Europe, reflecting differences in policy, market, energy, and industrial conditions. China's state-led approach has supported rapid market expansion, cost reductions, and industrial competitiveness, with local governments implementing targeted measures to promote battery-electric-vehicle adoption. In contrast, Europe relies more heavily on cooperation between public and private stakeholders, emphasizing lifecycle sustainability and cross-border infrastructure development. However, Europe's dependence on imported battery materials creates vulnerabilities within its supply chain.

title: GRIDS: An integrated sustainability framework for the net-zero transition
abstract: Net zero is not a single-sector decarbonisation problem: it spans energy, resource circularity, biodiversity, climate-aligned finance and supply-chain governance, and interventions in one domain register on the others. The review responds to a specific gap: these determinants are examined in separate literatures whose interactions are asserted rather than modelled. Following PRISMA 2020 conventions, this review consolidates twenty-four determinants into the GRIDS framework, comprising Governance and capital allocation, Resource circularity, Infrastructure and energy transition, Digitally enabled integration, and Stewardship of natural capital; nests them in eight validated clusters; and models their interdependence rather than asserting it. Fifty-three studies anchor the digital domain in oil and gas. A directed cross-impact matrix over the clusters is examined through MICMAC, interpretive structural modelling and perturbation simulation, as complementary lenses on one model rather than independent tests. Digital measurement and traceability are the only cluster whose independent classification survives boundary perturbation: it sits alone at the hierarchy's base, emitting strong links to six of the seven other clusters and receiving none, inverting the conventional treatment of digital tools as a service function. Ecological state and energy infrastructure jointly absorb perturbation from across the system, reported as a pair rather than ranked. The implication is a sequence: measurement layer first, energy build-out screened hardest, supply-chain and municipal outcomes last. The matrix is author-coded under a stated admissibility rule, not independently elicited, so these results are offered as falsifiable propositions released for re-elicitation. Priority gaps concern cross-domain metrics harmonisation, developing-economy applicability and AI governance.

title: A structured ex-post synthesis of Nordic power sector pathways from independently developed scenarios
abstract: Nordic energy planning draws on scenarios developed for different purposes, making it difficult to determine what their results support when considered together. A structured review of 63 studies relevant to comparing energy system models and scenarios identifies six study-design families and informs an ex-post synthesis of eight model-scenario cases from six model families. Ex-post synthesis documents recurring developments and contrasts, while attribution to particular assumptions requires a controlled comparison. The synthesis covers Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden in 2030, 2040 and 2050, retaining each case's identity and context. Between 2030 and 2050, onshore wind capacity increases by more than 0.1 GW in 20 of 21 eligible national trajectories, and solar PV capacity does so in 17. Modelled net onshore wind capacity additions by 2050 equal 11–654% of national total generating capacity in 2020. Total installed capacity varies approximately sevenfold in Finland, and technology portfolios differ substantially. In Norway, LUT-ESTM and OSeMBE report similar final electricity demand in 2050, at 218 and 220 TWh/yr, but 109 and 51 GW of onshore wind and 704 and 302 TWh/yr of power generation, respectively. Reported power-supply CO 2 emissions are numerically lower in 2050 than in 2030 in all 20 eligible trajectories, but zero and negative endpoints reflect different scenario targets, sectoral boundaries and accounting conventions. The pathways are therefore most useful as contrasting planning cases rather than as a common forecast. Nordic grid, permitting and spatial-planning decisions should consequently be assessed across several wind-deployment scales, with explicit assumptions about electricity use.

title: Blockchain-enabled strategic pathways for enhancing offshore wind energy supply chain resilience: An integrated decision-support framework
abstract: Offshore wind energy projects face disruptions due to their complexity and reliance on the global supply chain (SC), making SC resilience vital for the reliable and sustainable development of offshore wind energy. Blockchain could enhance resilience through transparency, asset tracking and information security. To strengthen the resilience of offshore wind energy SCs, this study aims to apply an integrated decision-support framework for identifying and prioritizing strategic blockchain-enabled pathways. Drawing on a review of the literature on offshore wind energy SCs, resilience and blockchain applications, the criteria are specified. Then SWOT analysis is used to formulate blockchain-based strategies. The Fuzzy Stepwise Weight Assessment Ratio Analysis (F-SWARA) and Fuzzy Measurement Alternatives and Ranking according to the COmpromise Solution (F-MARCOS) technique were used to rank the suggested strategies. To assess robustness, sensitivity analyses were conducted on criteria weights and expert weights and a comparison was performed using fuzzy decision-making techniques. Economic value and reduction of disruption costs, implementation and maintenance cost and traceability and visibility of equipment and data were the most important sub-criteria. Also, the strategies of developing a blockchain-based intelligent decision-making platform to increase SC resilience in disruption conditions, establishing a blockchain-based risk management and early warning system for SC disruptions and implementing a blockchain-based equipment tracking system were identified as the most significant proposed strategies, respectively. These findings provide context-specific insights that may inform offshore wind developers, policymakers, and SC stakeholders when considering blockchain investments and resilience-enhancing initiatives under resource and infrastructure constraints. • Introducing a strategic framework for offshore wind supply chain resilience. • Developing blockchain strategies in offshore wind projects using SWOT analysis. • Applying Fuzzy SWARA-MARCOS methods for evaluating identified strategies. • Robustness assessment using sensitivity analysis and comparison with MCDM methods. • Offering policy and managerial insights for resilient offshore wind supply chains.

title: Geospatial analysis for optimal solar power plant siting in industrial zones
abstract: This study integrates Geographic Information Systems (GIS) with the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) to optimally identify locations for the establishment of solar power plants within Industrial zones across Iran. The principal innovation of this research lies in its evaluation of industrial zones as open land suitable for utility-scale, ground-mounted solar power plant deployment. Unlike most previous studies, which have primarily focused on undeveloped natural land such as barren or agricultural areas or built structures such as rooftops and dam reservoirs, this study emphasizes the strategic value of existing industrial infrastructure in solar power plant siting. For this purpose, eleven key criteria in three domains technical, economic, and environmental were carefully weighted and analyzed using AHP method. After conducting spatial modeling and integrating the layers within the ArcGIS environment, the total solar potential of the country was determined. The results indicated that the provinces of Kerman (5430 TWh/year), Sistan and Baluchestan (4937 TWh/year), Razavi Khorasan (4583 TWh/year), and Fars (4448 TWh/year) possess the highest theoretical capacities for solar energy production. Additionally, the analysis of overlap between industrial zones and high-radiation areas revealed that provinces such as Yazd, Kerman, Isfahan, and Qom demonstrate more than 60% overlap, offering substantial potential for the successful implementation of solar projects. These findings provide a strategic framework for renewable energy policymaking at the national level, as well as valuable insights for private sector decision-making in solar energy investments.

title: Coordinating shared flexibility in renewable-rich power systems: A structured critical review from a sharing-economy perspective
abstract: Renewable-dominated power systems increasingly rely on flexible assets owned by households, fleets, energy communities, and firms. Installed capacity alone does not make these resources available to the system because their operating states, primary uses, and owners’ willingness to participate change over time. In this review, shared flexibility refers to temporary access to the flexibility services of independently owned assets without transferring asset ownership. Such access may be coordinated through aggregators, energy communities, peer-to-peer platforms, or operator procurement. The asset owner, scheduling entity, service buyer, and settlement party may therefore be different actors. This review examines stationary and shared storage, electric vehicles, flexible demand, microgrids, and multi-energy resources across four connected dimensions: the capability that owners make available, the allocation of information and scheduling responsibility, the updating and dispatch of contracted flexibility across timescales, and the distribution of value, cost, and non-delivery risk. The literature shows that aggregation improves market access but does not by itself establish resource sharing. A workable arrangement must specify the service being offered, preserve network and resource feasibility, define the owner’s participation and override conditions, and link payment to measured delivery. Existing studies address these requirements unevenly, and few follow shared flexibility from resource commitment through dispatch to settlement. The review identifies the need for service-specific capability contracts, coordination models that retain owner autonomy while assigning operational responsibility, and settlement mechanisms that account for delivery performance and the cause of deviations.

title: Unraveling implementation gaps in China's urban climate pioneers: A decomposition analysis and its implications for latecomers
abstract: Pioneering urban trials represent the frontier of global climate mitigation. China has strategically deployed three batches of low-carbon pilot cities to accelerate nationwide decarbonization through ambitious targets. Yet it remains unclear whether these pledges have translated into effective implementation. This study combines KPI benchmarking, Tapio-LMDI analysis, and counterfactual simulations to assess 71 pilot cities. Results reveal a systematic gap between overall mitigation trends and city-level policy delivery. While average energy and carbon intensities declined by more than 30% from 2010 to 2021, 37% of cities failed to meet carbon intensity targets, and 51% missed their non-fossil energy goals. This shortfall was proportionally higher in later-batch cities, where fossil energy reliance, including thermal power generation, remained a predominant factor in emission trajectories. Decomposition shows that the expansion of non-fossil energy plays a critical role in alleviating such constraints and is becoming increasingly important for achieving deep decarbonization and decoupling. Counterfactual analysis further indicates that fully closing the implementation gaps could have avoided over 310 Mt CO 2 (an 8% reduction compared to actual 2021 emissions), with 85% of this mitigation potential concentrated in third-batch cities and could have enabled universal decoupling. These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of urban decarbonization depends not only on target ambition but also on strict compliance and structural transition. Bridging the implementation gap is therefore essential to avert structural decarbonization delays in developing economies.

title: Strategic energy management of renewable-integrated EV charging and battery swapping systems for resilient distribution networks under uncertainty
abstract: The growing deployment of electric vehicles (EVs) and renewable energy sources (RES) brings about a substantial variability in demand and generation, which poses challenges for the reliable and coordinated operation of the distribution network. In this paper, a distributionally robust resilience-aware multi-objective optimization framework is proposed for the coordinated operation of renewable-integrated electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs) and battery swapping systems (BSSs) in radial distribution networks. The framework co-optimizes EV charging, battery swapping, renewable utilization, and resilience-aware operation under the uncertainties of renewable generation and EV demand while respecting the AC power-flow constraints. In the multi-objective formulation, network power loss, voltage deviation, carbon emissions, energy not supplied (ENS), service shortage, operating profit, and charging fairness are taken into account. The resilience is assessed using contingency-based ENS and uncertain operating conditions are handled using distributionally robust optimization (DRO). The proposed framework is tested on the IEEE 69-bus distribution system under different operating scenarios. The results demonstrate a network power loss of 2.56 MWh, minimum bus voltages are in the range of 0.944-0.965 p.u., about 24% carbon emission reduction and 0.97 MWh ENS in the considered contingency. Fairness index of Jain is more than 0.90 which is fair charging-resource allocation. The hypervolume (HV) and inverted generational distance (IGD) of the Pareto solution set obtained by the adaptive self-tuning cheetah optimization algorithm (AST-COA) are 0.842 and 0.021, respectively. The robustness of optimization results is verified by statistical analysis. The proposed framework shows the ability to reliably and co-ordinately operate EVCS-BSS under uncertain and contingency situations.

title: Fifteen years of China's electric vehicle market: Findings from an EEMD analysis of sales data
abstract: Understanding the temporal evolution of electric vehicle (EV) markets is critical for designing effective diffusion pathways and supportive policy frameworks. This study conducts an Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (EEMD) analysis of China's monthly EV sales data from January 2011 to December 2025, aiming to characterize market dynamics across multiple temporal scales and identify critical co-evolving events. The log-transformed sales series is decomposed into five stable intrinsic mode functions and one residual using EEMD, which are then reconstructed into short-, medium-, and long-term components through a period-based strategy. Variations in the reconstructed components are examined alongside representative policy, technology, and market events to interpret the historical context of China's EV market development. Results show that the long-term component maintains an upward trend, with its growth increment peaking around 2016 and moderating thereafter. The medium-term component exhibits periodic rises and falls, coinciding with industrial plans, technological breakthrough, and policy stringency. The short-term component captures seasonal fluctuations and local deviations that coincide with safety incidents, policy transitions, and the pandemic disruption. The findings suggest a multi-scale policy framework that emphasizes long-term support for market infrastructure, medium-term guidance on industrial and technological plans, and short-term measures to alleviate public concerns about EV safety and perceived policy uncertainty.

title: Do energy shocks accelerate green credit? Evidence from Chinese banks in the Asian energy transition
abstract: This study examines how energy uncertainty shapes green credit allocation in China, a major Asian economy where banks play a central role in financing the low-carbon transition. Against the backdrop of rising energy-market volatility, geopolitical disruptions, and growing pressure to strengthen energy security, the paper investigates whether energy uncertainty constrains bank lending or encourages a reallocation of credit toward greener activities. To strengthen identification, the empirical strategy combines fixed-effects estimation with an instrumental-variable approach using geopolitical risk and dynamic panel GMM estimators, allowing endogeneity and persistence in green credit behavior to be addressed from complementary angles. Using a balanced panel of Chinese commercial banks, the results indicate that energy uncertainty significantly increases banks’ green credit ratios, suggesting that banks respond to energy shocks by reallocating credit toward environmentally sustainable sectors rather than uniformly reducing lending. This effect persists during energy shocks and periods of increased demand for green projects, indicating that the response is stronger among market-oriented banks, including joint-stock and city commercial banks, which appear more flexible in adjusting their loan portfolios. The study offers important implications for Asian economies seeking to align financial stability, energy security, and sustainable development objectives.

title: Power system expansion in Ecuador: A stakeholder driven sustainability assessment of generation technologies
abstract: Ecuador experienced severe power shortages in 2024, with blackouts lasting up to 14 h a day, exposing the vulnerability of an electricity system that relies heavily on hydroelectric plants, is affected by drought, and has seen limited investment in new capacity since 2018. In this context, the central government has begun promoting nuclear energy as a medium- and long-term option, despite the country’s lack of experience with this technology and the Electricity Master Plan’s identification of substantial renewable potential. This study provides a sustainability assessment of eight generation technologies for Ecuador’s future energy mix: PV-US, geothermal, onshore wind, biomass, combined-cycle gas turbines, mini hydropower, small modular nuclear reactors, and conventional nuclear fission. The analysis is supported by Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis methods using ELECTRE III and HELDA (Helmholtz MCDA Tool), based on a performance matrix with 15 static baseline sustainability criteria grouped into environmental, technical, economic, and social categories, and weightings derived from a 35-stakeholder survey across the public, private, and academic sectors. Results show that stakeholders rank the availability of domestic resources as the most important criterion, followed by the levelized cost of electricity, risk to human health, and investment costs. When technologies are ranked using these weighted criteria, four renewable options (mini hydropower, onshore wind, PV-US, and geothermal) are preferred, followed by combined-cycle gas turbines and biomass, while both nuclear options are consistently ranked at the bottom. These results recommend that energy policy decisions in Ecuador should be based on transparent, stakeholder-driven assessments of technological options, rather than unilateral decisions detached from stakeholder preferences and system realities.

title: Prioritizing transport decarbonization strategies in Nigeria: An intuitionistic fuzzy decision framework for energy transition policy
abstract: Nigeria's transport sector is a major and growing source of Greenhouse Gas (GHG) emissions, largely because mobility remains heavily dependent on petroleum products. Efforts to shift toward low-carbon transport are hindered by economic, institutional, infrastructural, and technological constraints. This study develops an integrated decision framework for prioritizing these challenges and identifying suitable policy responses within Nigeria's wider energy transition. Drawing on the literature, national policy documents, and the judgments of six experts from academia, government, transport, and energy, the study evaluates eight decarbonization challenges and five policy alternatives. It proposes an Intuitionistic Fuzzy (IF) extension of the RANking COMparison method (IF-RANCOM) to determine the relative importance of the challenges while considering uncertainty and hesitation in expert judgments. The resulting weights are incorporated into an Intuitionistic Fuzzy Additive Ratio Assessment (IF-ARAS) model to evaluate the policy alternatives. Compromise Fuzzy Ranking (CFR) is then used to reconcile differences among expert assessments and produce a collective ranking. The findings identify Nigeria's economic dependence on petroleum as the most important barrier, followed by weak policy frameworks and planning, inadequate infrastructure and technological capacity, and the high cost of zero-emission vehicles. Promoting mass transit is ranked as the most suitable policy response. Comparative and sensitivity analyses reveal that the main rankings remain stable under different methodological assumptions and parameter settings. The findings demonstrate the need for coordinated investment in mass transit, integrated transport and land use planning, sustainable financing, infrastructure modernization, and institutional reform. The proposed framework may also support other fossil-fuel-dependent developing economies in aligning transport priorities with energy security, social inclusion, and long-term decarbonization goals.

title: Financial development and the energy transition in China: Does green capital accelerate decarbonization?
abstract: China's dual carbon targets peak CO2 by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2060 place financial markets at the centre of the country's clean energy transition. This paper investigates whether financial development, and green finance in particular, accelerates decarbonization across China's 30 provinces over the period 2003 to 2022. A composite Financial Development Index (FDI) is constructed using principal component analysis from four dimensions: banking sector depth, stock market development, insurance market penetration, and green finance intensity (green credit ratio and green bond issuance). The analysis employs a two-way fixed-effects spatial Durbin model (SDM) with a queen-contiguity weight matrix to capture spatial spillovers, a double-threshold panel regression to identify nonlinear green finance effects, and a bootstrap mediation analysis to decompose transmission channels. Results demonstrate that a one-standard-deviation increase in the composite FDI reduces provincial CO2 emissions by 21.8% (direct effect) and generates a cross-provincial spillover reduction of 9.6%, for a total effect of 31.4%. Green finance exhibits the strongest individual sub-component effect, reducing emissions by 28.4% and displaying threshold behaviour: the decarbonization impact is insignificant below a green finance intensity ratio of 0.32, rises sharply in the intermediate regime (0.32 to 0.62), and intensifies further above 0.62 as capital allocation shifts systematically toward renewable energy and low-carbon technology. Mediation analysis identifies four significant channels technology innovation, renewable energy investment, industrial ecology upgrading, and energy efficiency improvement which together account for 21.3% of the total effect. Regional heterogeneity analysis reveals that the green finance channel is strongest in Eastern provinces, where capital markets are deepest, and weakest in Western provinces, suggesting a financial geography constraint on clean transition. The findings imply that accelerating green bond market development, expanding the green credit incentive framework, and closing cross-provincial financial integration gaps are essential policy levers for meeting the 2030 peak-emissions deadline.

title: Decarbonising road freight: A scoping review and conceptual framework for alternative fuel and powertrain selection
abstract: The transition to alternative fuels and powertrains is a critical lever for road freight decarbonisation. However, these technologies present complex techno-economic and environmental trade-offs, creating a need for strategic decision support on which technologies to adopt. This systematic scoping review analyses studies that apply quantitative decision-making methods to evaluate and select alternative fuels and powertrains. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, an initial 6,372 articles published from 2015 onwards were identified through database searching. After screening and citation searching, 45 primary studies were included in the review. The analysis reveals that exact optimisation (n = 27) is predominantly used for fleet planning or transport and energy system transition modelling, whereas multi-criteria decision-making (n = 15) is primarily applied for strategic technology ranking and prioritisation. Metaheuristic approaches (n = 3) are largely reserved for highly complex or computationally difficult optimisation problems. The evidence base is concentrated in Europe and North America, limiting the transferability of evidence to the Global South. Multiple research and modelling gaps were also identified that affect comparability and practical usability. These include unspecified contextual boundaries, limited social impacts, narrow environmental modelling, and unspecified fuel production pathways. The primary contribution of this review is the Alternative Fuel and Powertrain Decision Framework (AFPDF). This conceptual framework combines recurring decision elements across the evidence base with modelling and reporting recommendations to structure the broader decision-making process, whilst addressing existing gaps. The AFPDF provides analysts with a transparent process for generating context-specific fuel and powertrain recommendations for road freight stakeholders, and reporting the assumptions on which those recommendations depend.

title: Population aging, automation, and energy productivity in China: Can technology offset demographic decline?
